Ah, that's only true if whoever is in charge is willing to _have_ a bottleneck in reviewing. In some software development groups, there is a strong pressure for reviews to pass, i.e. expectation that reviewers approve; and the notion of veto is not common, so that if some reviewer objects, the implementing developer can find others who would be willing to accept, bypassing the objections. Also, few people are willing to conduct long reviews of a lot of code, and even less people are willing to read multiple comments in a long review of a lot of code.

Now, in some projects, there are only one or two "owners" or "marshals" for some areas of the code, so they can apply a strict standard if they want to, but - their time is limited, meaning that long LLM vibe-pull-requests are likely to either be ignored for a long time or rejected off-hand.

There are required exceptions to attorney client privilege[0]:

> the confidentiality rule is subject to limited exceptions. Paragraph (b)(1) recognizes the overriding value of life and physical integrity and permits disclosure reasonably necessary to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm

An eventual lawyer-bot probably should be able to identify this, however this does pose a conondrum.

If the lawyer gets told by the LLM "the client's words indicate there may be a threat to life that requires you report them to the police", there could be various liability associated with either path of action.

If the lawyer reports them to the police, but then the client challenges that on grounds of attorney-client privilege being broken, is "the LLM said it qualified" a valid reason that'll prevent the lawyer from being found at fault?

If they lawyer doesn't report them, but then the client commits said murder, would the lawyer be liable if their LLM transcript were admitted into evidence under the theory of "you should've listened to the LLM telling you that you had to report it"?

This is an inherent problem with giving LLMs (or computers in general!) any say over anything that threatens someone's life or liberty, even with a human in the loop. Same applies to the potential for AI-driven upcoding in hospital environments where a doctor has to weigh potentially ignoring the AI and then missing some diagnosis (Safest path is probably to run extra tests to check if the AI's theory is correct, but then that's still de-facto upcoding).

That's sort of a loaded question depending on what you mean by "smaller sub expert models inside".

At the most abstract level, you can observe patterns in a model's activations and theorize that particular collections of components contribute to particular kinds of operations. There are many flavors of this intuition. In that sense, you can think of there being "submodels" within a model, insofar as different parts of the network can participate in specialized computations. Some reading that might interest you in this area would include things like mechanistic interpretability.

There are also Mixture of Expert models, which are a dominant architecture for LLMs now, in which you essentially have a bunch of smaller FFNs that get routed over/aggregated together when the LLM performs a forward pass. It would be a mistake to treat any single expert as a better task specific model though. They are trained as part of an ensemble, and they're almost always being combined with other experts in the forward pass, so they're more like (to use a loose analogy) regions of the brain that tend to correspond more towards particular actions than others. You couldn't just extract one and say "This is now our Chess model that performs as well as the larger LLM we took it from". You could potentially use the relevant experts as a basis for training a smaller task-specific model, and there is work around expert pruning and other distillation techniques, but it's not as simple as "This smaller inner model is a complete task-specific model as is". And more importantly, that ensemble of experts *is* the LLM you're comparing it to, at least in major part. It doesn't really make sense to treat the LLM as some foreign model that calls the expert. The experts themselves don't often correlate to easily interpretable task domains, as they've been learned via joint computation with the other experts and broader LLM.

Then there's tool calling. Today LLMs are trained to make tool calls (basically execute functions) for particular tasks. Those tools can be smaller specialized models, or deterministic code, or anything really that can be fired from a host environment.

title: Show HN: Chkit – Schema, migrations and backfills for ClickHouse (like Drizzle)
text:
Hey HN, im Marc, co-founder of ObsessionDB. We are open sourcing ChKit, our tooling to manage schemas, migrations and backfills for clickhouse.

I am a big fan of the type safety drizzle provides for the database. Manage the schema in typescript and generate migrations from it is a powerful workflow. I always wished something like it would exist for clickhouse, so we could manage our analytical workloads the same way. It didn't exist, so we build it.

We build it after running ClickHouse at petabyte scale in our previous company, were we managed hundreds of tables, MVs and endpoints reading from them.

The way it works:

1. You define your schema in typescript, with typed helpers for tables, mv, column types etc.. 2. You generate the migration, that contains the DDL, to get your clickhouse instance from status quo to what your current typescript schema defines 3. Your CI can check for drift 4. You run the generated migration against production 5. You use the defined types in your code, to ingest your data while making sure it has the correct type. Bonus: if your schema change was BC breaking, we generate the sequence on how to backfill the data, into the intermediate table to migrate (this is quite the hard problem with large tables and schema evolution)

In case you have already a clickhouse instance with a schema, you can pull it down and start using ChKit from where you are.

Run our generator to setup the boilerplate:

  npm create chkit@latest
If you folks are running clickhouse in production, I am curious to hear what other challenges you are running into.
